preamble: Raising of the open back rounded vowel [ɒ(ː)] to open-mid [ɔ(ː)]. In 17th-century English the LOT vowel /ɒ/ was lengthened to /ɒː/ before voiceless fricatives in words such as off, cost and cloth, the start of the LOT–CLOTH split. In General American and old-fashioned Received Pronunciation this /ɒː/ was raised to /ɔː/, merging with THOUGHT; many accents of England restored short /ɒ/ instead, and that became standard RP by the mid-20th century. In present-day Standard Southern British the short LOT vowel itself, traditionally /ɒ/, has shifted upwards to about [ɔ]: younger speakers use a closer quality than older ones.

examples.from: off with the lengthened LOT vowel /ɒː/ (17th century)

examples.note: Present-day RP has short /ɒ/ again (/ɒf/, /klɒθ/, /kɒst/). American accents with the cot–caught merger have /ɑ/ in these words.

languageExamples.language: English (Received Pronunciation to Standard Southern British)

examples.note: Wikström (2013), cited in the RP article, finds that younger RP and near-RP speakers use a closer LOT vowel than older speakers, roughly intermediate between the older LOT and THOUGHT qualities. THOUGHT has moved up at the same time, to about [oː].
